utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution I'm Thomas Hannis along with our acting case manager Jasmina Bosnjakovic. And I would like to indicate that there's three brief procedural matters I would like to raise before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence appearing today Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The three matters: One relates to a witness yesterday at the transcript page number 6481 beginning at line 4, et cetera. Ms. Korner had referred to -- to document 65 ter 9020, which was an excerpt from the witness's suspect interview that she showed during re-direct examination, but I don't think it was tendered as an exhibit. She asked me to request that it be tendered for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honours, if -- what does it refer to? The excerpt of -- of witness's interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it was shown a page or two pages from the transcript of his interview and because it was shown in court, we felt that it should be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The ones which -- which Ms. Korner was reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yeah, yeah. I think Ms. Korner was actually reading from the document. She was reading into the transcript from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you're query is why does it have to be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct. But if that is -- if that particular passage is in question, is that what the Prosecution would like, if we can have some -- some -- some time during the course of the -- today's court that we can perhaps give our -- our position on -- during the break, or after the break, immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe the -- sorry. Maybe the Prosecution should simply just specify exactly which parts it is you wish to have exhibited. Whether it is only the parts that she read out or maybe the pages surrounding that little passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My understanding it was only the pages she read out, but if the Defence counsel can review the document and they are satisfied that she read it accurately, then I think we don't need to tender it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the second matter relates to a witness coming next week. The first witness scheduled next week is not scheduled to arrive until late Saturday night, as I understand it. He will be proofed by the Prosecution on Sunday. As a large number of documents and an audio of his prior taped interview as well as some intercepts to listen to, the gist of it is I think the Prosecution, Ms. Korner will take all day with him Sunday, and the Defence has requested to see him for, I believe, a couple of hours or three hours altogether. I think we're currently scheduled to sit on Monday morning, so the Prosecution would request for the witness's sake and the parties that if we could possibly have an afternoon sitting. I don't have if the courtroom is available or not. Or if not, begin the witness on Tuesday morning, rather than Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, were you nodding your head?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Yeah, yeah, it's okay with us, Your Honour, well, depending on the availability of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the Registry would advise us in the course of today as to the availability of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the counter it does currently look like Courtroom I is available in the afternoon, but we'll check. The third matter, Your Honour, the last matter relates to today's witness, the next witness. I had filed a motion yesterday to amend the 65 ter list to add two exhibits and seek to use those with your leave with this witness. One is a -- a map of the Pale area, and one is a payroll document from November 1992, which lists the names of various personnel in the state or national security of the RS MUP. I had asked Defence if they had any objection. Mr. Zecevic had indicated to me he did not, but I haven't heard back from the Zupljanin Defence yet as to their position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well [Microphone not activated] in respect of that motion. Late yesterday afternoon, the Prosecution filed a motion to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list to add two documents in relation to ST-211. As the Trial Chamber will deny the motion for reasons to be explained, the Defence will not be asked to respond. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution had -- has not fully argued the motion as required under the Rules. In particular, the Prosecution has not provided any arguments justifying the very late filing of the request. The Chamber notes that one of the two documents is a map, a document that likely will have been available to the Prosecution for a long time. The second document is a payroll document. The Prosecution does not make any attempt to establish that it has been diligent in seeking to add this document to its list, so the motion is hereby denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire? If it is simply the failure to explain what the relevance of the map is that led to the decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- I thought, Mr. Hannis, that the reasons sufficiently explain why the motion is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would indicate there are two Pale maps on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. However, they're less adequate for the purposes that I propose to show a map to this witness and that they are simply, one is more or less a schematic showing the roads in the Pale municipality. The other map is -- it is a poor quality copy. It does show downtown Pale and the police station and the cultural -- the former cultural centre of the gymnasium where some of the non-Serbs were detained, which is part of one of our scheduled incidents. But this witness, in his job, in the national security in providing protection for certain individuals, talks about the locations of hotels where those individuals stayed. I -- I thought it was helpful for his testimony. But I will do without it in light of your ruling. And with that, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Late yesterday, the Prosecution circulated by way of e-mail a proofing note of ST-211. At the end of that note, there is a paragraph where the Prosecution states that, and I quote: "In the event that the above information goes beyond the scope of the original Rule 65 ter summary for this witness, this proofing note is intended to amend that summary and to notify of the Prosecution's intent to lead the above evidence, subject to the approval of the Trial Chamber." The Trial Chamber has, in the past, cautioned the Prosecution on this matter of motions through informal means and will therefore not recognise the request made in the proofing note as a motion. However, given the formulation of the note, if the Prosecution intends to lead evidence beyond what is in the Rule 65 ter summary, it should provide arguments why the Chamber should grant such an expansion, and the Chamber would rule on it at that time. There is a third ruling that the -- that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, that -- that other matter [Microphone not activated] Sorry. That other matter we will deal with at a later stage. It concerns Witness ST-216.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just -- while Your Honours was giving the rulings, I checked the -- the e-court. 65 ter, the document which -- which Mr. Hannis wanted -- on behalf of Ms. Korner to introduce into evidence, is basically the whole -- the whole statement. 65 ter 9020 does not refer to the specific pages of the document but is his whole interview. Therefore, I mean, I'm not sure what is the -- the submission of the Prosecution. Do they want the whole interview in, or just -- or just a part --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My understanding it was only the portions that were read out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It was read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The point is if the Defence has any disagreement about whether or not she read it out accurately, then I think we would need to show with the page as to what he actually said. If she read it out accurately, there's not need to put in an excerpt from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I -- as far as I remember, Ms. Korner was reading accurately, but she was jumping from one thing to the other. So basically we wouldn't have a problem if this particular part, these two or three pages, are -- are -- are offered as exhibit. But then I think that the Prosecution would actually have to make a -- an excerpt from his interview of these relevant pages and offer that and then we can give our final position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hannis, you will refine the application that you're actually making so we know what it is the Prosecution is seeking to exhibit. Is that where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will ask Ms. Korner to deal with that and verify whether or not what she read in was accurate. If that is, the transcript can stand as it is and there doesn't need to be any admission of the 65 ter document in whole or in part, because I think what she wanted is in evidence, in the transcript. So I will check with her, and we will get back to you. With regard to your most recent decision on the Prosecution's proofing note, I'm sorry, I don't have it in front of me, but very early on in the case, I had a witness where an issue arose during proofing where in my view it was -- it was a close call as to whether or not what he had raised was outside the scope of the 65 ter summary. In erring on the side of caution, I filed a motion asking that we be permitted to amend the 65 ter and lead that evidence. And at that time Your Honours indicated -- I guess you felt that I didn't need to file that motion, that it didn't go outside the scope. Now, the 65 ter summary for this witness is in rather broad terms, and so, again, I think I took the cautious approach and indicated that if the determination was this new information goes beyond the scope then I would seek permission to lead it because I believe it is important evidence. It deals with what has been a contested issue in this case and I think will continue to be a continued issue. And in the 65 ter summary for this witness it says: "By the nature of his position in the RS MUP, that position was chief of administration for security of persons and facilities in the State Security Service, the witness will provide evidence of the workings of the State Security Service." This new evidence in particular relates to what we say is the personal security that was provided for Minister Stanisic and that was being provided by someone or -- some other group rather than the state security personnel. We say it was Dusko Malovic and his Special Police platoon. I guess I need to know from Your Honours whether you see that as being beyond the scope of the 65 ter summary. If it is not, then can I lead the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it will -- it will always be the case that the appreciation of counsel on one side, or counsel on the other side, or the Chamber, might not be identical as to whether something is new and therefore could be led, or something is wholly outside the scope of what were the -- the other side had been put on notice in relation to. And the Chamber is not going to attempt to -- to give a -- a general anticipatory ruling in these matters because it can't. What it says is, in this case, that note appearing at the bottom of a proofing note was not a motion, A; and B, what was, it appeared to us, that this was the type of new material which required a motion, a proper motion. That's all he said. And you would -- I would remind you, as to the ruling in this respect, that we will consider a motion when it is made. But there is no motion before -- there is no proper motion before the Chamber at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that case I would seek leave to make an oral application to you at this time to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I call on the other side to respond to your motion without notice in the proper sense, what are the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reasons are, Your Honour, I first learned of there evidence yesterday when I proofed the witness after having met him for the first time. When he was interviewed in June of 2009 by the Prosecution he was interviewed by investigator Paul Grady. If you saw the interview you would see much of the focus in that interview is related more to the Karadzic case than this case. This witness worked in providing personal security in the RS MUP for high individuals like Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, the prime minister, et cetera. So the focus was more on that. He was not asked about who provided security for Mico Stanisic. In interviewing him, I asked that question. He told me, We did not. I said, Who did? And that's where the information came in about Dusko Malovic. So as soon as I learned of it, I put it in the proofing note, forwarded it to the Defence, and now I'm making my application. You will have noted on one of our organisational charts for the RS MUP for April through December 1992, we have Mico Stanisic at the top, the Prosecution has drawn a line out to the right to the Sokolac Special Police platoon or company, I can't remember how it is designated on the chart. This was a matter, I think we told Your Honours about early on when we were trying to reach agreement with the Defence about the organisational charts, and this is one that the -- that the Stanisic Defence took issue with. We say that this group was under the direct supervision of the minister, and the Defence has been denying that and saying, as I understand it, that they were not related to the minister in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness was interviewed on the 4th of May, 2009, a month before the Prosecution submitted their pre-trial brief --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I should correct Mr. Zecevic. If he checks, May 4th was the first contact with the witness, but the interview was not carried out at that time because there was an issue about his status as a suspect. He requested an attorney. The full interview did not take place until the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But the situation is only worse in that case, because in our view, the explanation is not good enough of the fact that was not asked about it. On the 6th of June 2009, we were supposed to already commence the trial. We were supposed to start in the summer, but we started in September, and the Prosecution was duty-bound to ask the witness about all the relevant facts for which he was being called as a witness in this case, so that's why we oppose it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a response from counsel for Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we endorse what our learned friend Mr. Zecevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may make a brief reply. I would indicate to that you the remedy, if you think of remedy as necessary, is to allow the Defence more time to prepare for cross-examination rather than exclude this element -- this evidence which we say is important and relevant to you. You should admit the evidence but give the Prosecution -- the Defence more time if that's what they need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I suppose I should have asked that were the Chamber inclined to grant the application on the understanding that the Defence would require more time, how much time would you consider reasonable for the Defence to deal with this new material?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- I -- I don't know what -- what the -- what the evidence will be. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, you have it in summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the proofing -- in the proofing note. Yes, but it depends what is the scope of -- of the -- of the -- of the direct examination of the witness and what specific data or details will be -- would the witness give. Now, only then I will be able to -- to assess -- assess the time that I need. But I assume that I would -- I would need just maybe a couple of hours preparation, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could we just inquire whether your -- whether the new information that has been revealed is that this witness was not a member of the Sokolac SJB Special Police platoon which is depicted in your chart. Where does this -- so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, this witness was not a member of the Sokolac platoon. He was a member of the national security, and he was a head of what was called the 5th Administration which was responsible for security of persons and facilities. But he is going to testify that he and his group provided protection for the Presidency for the National Assembly for the prime minister. But they did not provide personal protection for Minister Stanisic. That was being done by Dusko Malovic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So there's nothing new really for what -- I mean -- because this chart seems to suggests that it was Drago Malovic who provided protection to Mr. Stanisic, and that's exactly what the witness today has confirmed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. But up to now it's just the chart. This is a living person who is going to say, I was there, my responsibility was personal protection. We didn't do it. I saw Dusko Malovic with the minister going to see Karadzic and Krajisnik and -- that's new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just for us to understand, what this witness is going to confirm today is actually is that this map is correct. Is that how we are do understand it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He is going -- I don't know that he can make that conclusion. I think he with provide an opinion that that's what this group was doing on the occasions he saw them, given that he himself is somewhat of an expert on personal protection because that was his job for years, and can he testified about seeing these men in camouflage with weapons escorting Mr. Stanisic when he came to the building across the street and that's the building where Karadzic and Krajisnik had offices, and he saw that three or four occasions in Pale. That's the evidence he's going to present. We think that's pretty good evidence about that issue, and it's better than just a line on the chart, because the Defence didn't agree to that line on the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence still doesn't agree with the line on the chart, but the point of the matter, Your Honours, is that we understood the -- the Prosecutor's case to be, and the chart, the specific chart, that you were just showing that this special unit from Sokolac was under the auspices of the minister the very same way as the special brigade headed -- commanded by Mr. Karisik and that is the case of -- that was the case of the Office of the Prosecutor so far as I understood it and from the pre-trial brief and from the last six months. Now, this is a completely new piece of information for us that actually the allegation from the -- from -- from the Office of the Prosecutor is that Malovic's unit was actually providing protection for Mr. Stanisic. I would like -- I would like my learned friend to -- to state to us what is the nature of their case so we would be able to -- to deal with that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you want to hear from me? First of all, I think my learned friend incorrectly states it when we said that this group is under the auspices of the minister the very same way the special brigade commanded by Mr. Karisik was. Mr. Karisik and the special brigade were specially provided for and they are in the orders and in the instructions. We don't have a document like that about this group, and our position is this was much more informal ad hoc, and we don't have a document showing them under the law on the ministry, and we don't see a provision for such a group. We don't see a decision establishing this group. So we say this was more ad hoc. This seemed to be his personal choice and these were his guys. Not only doing personal security, but we believe we'll present evidence later on that they did other things as well besides personal security including perhaps being involved in one of the -- a crime that has been discussed that was sought to be added to the indictment is not a charged Defence but the Prosecution was under the impression that we are allowed to lead evidence about that later on to the extent that it shows knowledge, lack of mistake, command and control, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber grants the motion of the Prosecution in this regard to allow this -- to allow the Prosecution to lead this additional evidence from the Witness ST-211 and will hold itself alert to such application as counsel for the Defence may make in terms of needing more time to deal with its cross-examination. So the witness may be -- the usher may --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- escort the witness to the stand. [Microphone not activated] ... alerted -- sorry. Thank you. While the witness is coming in we have just been alerted that the court management and support services confirms that it is possible to move this case to the afternoon of Monday, the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will notify all the interested parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This option was -- was suggested in order to provide an opportunity for the Defence, if -- in case they need more time to have Monday morning to discuss it with their clients so as we can continue on Monday afternoon. But, of course, if you in the end you don't think you need extra time to carry out your cross-examination with this witness, then, there's no need to move the session on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe Your Honours, the session on Monday afternoon was -- was related to a new coming witness, not this witness. But the witness who is -- who is -- who is only coming on Saturday, late in the night, and then the Defence is meeting him on Sunday morning, but that would sort of limit the time for the preparation of our learned friend's need for that witness. So it doesn't have anything to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. But could I nevertheless inquire as to whether now that we know the availability of the courtroom, the Prosecution -- this is -- that is -- that you're in fact making, or you were alerting us that you may be making it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is our request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't oppose, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're not opposing that request from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So when we take the adjournment tomorrow we will resume at 2.15 on Monday afternoon. That is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... a new witness because I anticipate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... with the new witness. Now the other point that Judge Harhoff raises is we may still have to come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the original time estimated for the Prosecution with this witness was four hours. I think I will take two hours or less. I have talked to Mr. Zecevic and he indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If this concerns my inability to state how much time for this additional evidence that this witness is providing I might need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the concern of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are we sitting in the morning or the afternoon tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm certainly not objecting to Mr. Zecevic having overnight to prepare for this limited bit of evidence that's new. I mean, if he is finished with everything else at 5.00 we can start with his other counsel and he can have overnight. I think that's reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. You are very considerate. I would like to rest a bit during the night, but I understand and I appreciate. Now, Your Honours, definitely overnight will be more than enough time for me to prepare for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, please, swear in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. And thank you for coming to this Tribunal to give your testimony today. Before I explain to you the proceedings, I would like you to state your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milan Scekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scekic. When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1st January, 1951, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was your occupation at the relevant time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree in law, and in 1992 I was working in the CSB Sarajevo as chief of security, in charge of providing security for persons and facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you of your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, have you ever testified before in this Tribunal or in any other national jurisdiction in relation to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the statement I gave to the OTP investigators, this is the first time I'm giving evidence anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I will just briefly explain to you how the proceedings are going to unfold here for you. You are being called as a witness for the Prosecution, who is sitting to your right, and the Prosecution has asked for, all together, four hours to take you through its examination-in-chief. I now understand that Mr. Hannis was going to be the counsel for the Prosecution, will use less than four hours. And when Mr. Hannis has completed his examination-in-chief, it will be for the Defence of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin to do their cross-examination, and I believe that the Defence for Mr. Stanisic has asked for - how much time, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We asked two and a half hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We asked for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just one half hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Scekic, there is an issue that has just arisen relating to some new evidence that was revealed during the proofing session that you had with the Prosecution a couple of days ago. In order to cover this new information, the Defence for Mr. Stanisic may wish to ask for more time to conduct its cross-examination, or, rather, may wish to have some time to prepare for its cross-examination, but we hope that we will still be able to complete your entire testimony by the end of tomorrow's session. At the end of the cross-examination by the Defence counsels, the Judges may also wish to put some questions to you and, of course, there will also be an opportunity for the Prosecution to put a few questions to you in re-examination after the completion of the Defence counsels' cross-examination. We will have a break every 90 minutes because the tapes for the recording of these proceedings need to be changed, so every one hour and a half there will be a 20 minutes' break, and the sessions here, the hearings shall have to adjourn at 7.00 tonight, and then we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, also in this courtroom. I now give you -- give the floor to Mr. Hannis, who will begin his examination-in-chief, and if at any point you need to take a break or to put a question to you relating to your testimony, then please do not hesitate. There's one more caution that I wish to bring to you, and that is, to observe a small pause between the questions and the answers. This is not so much a problem when the Prosecution is examining you because you do not speak the same language, but when it comes to the Defence cross-examination, it is very easy for people who speak the same language just to answer and -- and ask questions overlapping each other and that will make it impossible for the interpreters to offer a solid interpretation of what is being said in the courtroom. So just take it easy, and be brief in your answers as much as you can. Mr. Hannis, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Scekic. I have difficulty pronouncing your name so I will probably just call you witness. You said you retired. When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you retire from? What was your profession?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a trained lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for whom did you work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I worked at the service of security, state security, in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the CSB of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you began your service with the state security in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I had a scholarship from the State Security Service, and I started working in 1979 in a centre that covered ten urban and ten peripheral municipalities, which made the work of the CSB rather complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your office was physically located where during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: My office was in central Sarajevo, almost -- in the building of the Republic Ministry of the Interior. The two buildings next to each other. First I worked on defence preparations, in the Republic Secretariat for Internal Affairs. That's what it was called now -- then, and then we moved into the building on the Zdravko Sotra Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I forgot there was one thing I wanted to mention early on. Before coming here to The Hague to testify as a witness, you had previously been summons for an interview in May of last year, 2009, as a suspect, and interviewed further on the 6th of June by representatives of the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you understand now, today, you're appearing before this Tribunal simply as a witness and only a witness? Not as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you for asking that question. There are a lot of unpleasant situations one encounters in life, and for me, such a situation was this invitation, or the summons, that I received in June last year. First of all, I couldn't understand a word of it. Should I clarify for the Trial Chamber? In the second interview, the investigators apologised to me saying the wording was very unfortunate, and that's how we proceeded, and if more explanation is necessary, I can provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions about that. The other lawyers or the Judges may later on. If I may, can I turn to your career in the MUP. During that interview, I know you mentioned something that you considered the high point of your career. Could you tell us briefly when and what that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: In the course of my work for the State Security Service I was chief of security for persons and facilities. I was appointed to that post in 1983. I was very professional in my job. The work of the State Security Service was lawful. It was based on the rules of procedure of the State Security Service, which rules were the groundwork for all the State Security Services in Yugoslavia. I received adequate financial remuneration and even some decorations, and the Crown piece of my work was during the Winter Olympics games in Sarajevo in 1984 for which I received special honours for my service. We had a strict hierarchy in the MUP, almost like in the army and we observed it strictly like soldiers. We did not, however, enjoy certain benefits that normal people do. We couldn't, for instance take an overdraft in the bank, which was normal for other people. We couldn't play games like wheels of fortune where you make a payment and then copy the receipt five times and send it to five different addresses. Some people won cars that way, whereas we received a curricular letter saying that employees of the State Security Service were not allowed to play that game. I'm just giving you this as an illustration of our great respect for -- for our management and the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: We observed them very strictly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to interrupt you there. I think you answered my question. And in 1984, you had only been in the MUP for five years, and you were involved in providing security for the Olympic Games; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Even when I was working on defence preparations, I achieved a very good performance that recommended me to -- to the organs who had appointed me in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. I want to ask you, in 1990 and 1991, were you still working in the centre in Sarajevo, in -- in your administration for protection of persons and facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let me just correct you, it was just a section whereas the administration was at the level of the Republic Secretariat for Internal Affairs, what we call MUP. But that doesn't matter. The Sarajevo centre was the strongest in the republic, and everything that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina that mattered happened mainly in the capital, Sarajevo. Yes, I was working there in 1990 and 1991, but the circumstances had changed. Did I go to work but nobody asked me what I was doing, nor did I ask any questions of anyone. After the multi-party elections, things went haywire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll get into that in a little bit. Who was your -- who was your boss? Who was your immediate superior in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior in 1991 was Borisa Delic, I think, or was it Slobodan Skipina -- no, no, Borisa Delic. Slobodan Skipina was the head of the security services centre in 1990. And at the time of multi-party elections, Munir Alibabic came to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you anticipated my next question. I think the name of the position at that time in 1990/1991 was the under-secretary for state security, and the transcript shows that you said the name was Slobodan, but we didn't catch the last name. Could you repeat that for us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was -- if it was interpreted well. Under-secretary in the State Security Service was Resid Music and Skipina was the chief of the State Security Centre because the centre had two sectors. The centre had two sectors: The public security sector and the state security centre. The chief of the state security sector in 1999 -- in 1990 in Sarajevo was Slobodan Skipina. The chief of the state security was Borisa Delic, and I think Mirza Grabonjic was the chief of the public security sector, but I'm not sure of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question then deals with the organisation within the State Security Service in 1991 and early 1992. In your interview you talked about lines of work or administrations that were numbered 01 through 07 or 08. Could you briefly number those for us and tell us what each one related to? 01 was what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Line 1 dealt with foreign intelligence services. Line 2 dealt with hostile immigration. Line 03 dealt with the enemy within. Line 04 dealt with technology. Line 05 dealt with defence preparations. Line 06 dealt with the security of persons and facilities. Line 07 was the analysis department. And line 08 was the sporting services -- support services. Somewhere in the text will you see also the lines of work of 05, 06 but they all have to do with the security of persons and facilities. The classification, as it existed, was the same for the entire Yugoslavia. Now, whether the security of persons was 05 or 06 and whether analysis really had that number or not, overall I don't know, but the lines as I described them applied to Sarajevo. At the level of the Ministry of the Interior, you had administrations matching these numbers. So line 01 which dealt with the same kind of issues. Line 02, et cetera, and the heads of administrations were inspectors who co-ordinated that line, various lines of work. And through various circulars, they suggested how work should be done. So within the ministry you had administrations which covered the work of all the centres throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and the centres were in Sarajevo, Mostar, Zenica, Gorazde, Tuzla, Banja Luka, Bihac and -- I think there were eight. I don't know if I have neglected to mention one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said last. The interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, witness, the interpreters said they couldn't hear the last thing you said and ask if you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Doboj. Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah, thank you. Now I understand that you've been talking about the state security side of the ministry. On the public security side, did they also have lines of work or administrations in their organisational structure? But they weren't the same ones you had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. They had a different organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And some of those included the police administration, the administration for crime prevention, things like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You made reference to this earlier, sir, that after the multi-party elections things began to take a turn for the worse in the Ministry of Interior. Is it fair to say that one of the reasons for that was because a number of non-professionals were being appointed to high positions within the MUP based on political affiliation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I think that the main problem lay in the Serbian Democratic Party, which, following multi-party elections, came out of the agreement with the other two parties holding the baby. Or it simply didn't know what it was -- which post it was supposed to take in the Ministry of Interior, because the Ministry of Interior did provide levers of power. If you get the post of a speaker of parliament as opposed to the prime minister's post then you know that the government is the one that creates policies then it is much better to have the post of a prime minister than that of speaker of the parliament because the government is the one drafting legislation or bills and forwarding them to the parliament. Then you wouldn't get very important posts on the government, like that of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Ministry of Defence. Instead, you were given some peripheral ministries or perhaps not peripheral but at any rate it is it much more important to hold a post of a minister of finance who is practically Deputy Prime Minister than to hold a post of a ministry of education and culture. I'm not saying that it is less important. But under the circumstances it was much more important --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm just talking about within the Ministry of the Interior. Would you agree that part of the problem was that non-professionals were being appointed to high positions within the MUP, and based on political affiliations, whether it was with the SDA, the HDZ, or the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. An individual was appointed to the post of the Ministry of the Interior who was of a rather suspicious past who used to work as a police officer in one of the police stations of the city of Sarajevo and came to the post of the ministry only because he was a member of the SDS. Also, on the Serb side, there were individuals who were appointed to high positions, and I did not believe that they were qualified for that. And I'm primarily referring to Mr. Vito Zepinic who does hold a doctoral degree, and I do have every respect for his scholarly work. But if you come across a problem and you address him for a solution, he could only shrug his shoulders, and I did not find that helpful. I told him, I'm approaching you because I would like you to solve my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The Serb personnel --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need to try and keep your answers short and focussed on my question. And I have to indicate, I think maybe one of your answers was -- was incorrectly translated. At line 16 through 18. You mentioned the post of the minister of the interior, an individual got appointed who had a suspicious past and came to the post only because he was a member of the SDS. I think you're referring to the SDA there. Am I correct? When you were talking about the person with the suspicious past.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right. It's an error perhaps in interpretation. He was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. But from the rest of your answer, I gather you are agreeing with me the problem was -- was on all three sides, that political people were being put into professional police jobs and many of these were people who had no prior experience or training to be police officers or police officials.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps they did have some experience, but there were other individuals who had more extensive experience than them. If you look at the persons who were appointed to posts within the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina compared to the individuals who worked in the State Security Service under the classification of jobs there were 120 posts. And there were only a handful of these individuals who were appointed to posts in the ministry, and they had hardly assumed their positions before they were replaced. There was one top-quality professional and one of the extensive individuals in the State Security Service who was one such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I understand you feel strongly about this, and I -- but I will need to try and keep you -- or ask you to keep your answer limited to my question. And I think this comes through in -- in your answers, that this situation caused a lot of dissatisfaction within the MUP on the part of you all -- from all ethnicities who had been working there as professionals before the multi-party elections. Would you agree with that, that this situation caused a lot of dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. And if I can make -- give you one more example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If it's brief, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Will be brief, and I've already related it to you. Since the under-secretary for state security of the former Yugoslavia was a post based on the parity principle, once Mr. Mustafic {as interpreted] term of office who was from Croatia expired, Sredoje Novic was pointed, however, as certain personnel officers came to the Ministry of the Interior, this person who was supposed to be the under-secretary was appointed to the Novi Grad municipal SUP and, of course, this was a terrible demotion and degradation for him, and Sredoje Novic is now, for instance, minister for civil affairs in the ministerial council of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you're being asked to speak more slowly when you answer. And would it be fair to say that all of this was also causing some suspicion and division between the different ethnicities who were employed within the MUP in 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your interview, I believe, that you became aware of talk within the MUP about forming a separate Serbian MUP. Can you tell us when you first became aware that there was talk like that? Approximately. If you can give us a month or a season of the year.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard of it was in 1992, in late March or earlier April, more likely. When I came out into the street and met two of my colleagues, I cannot recall their names. They asked me if I wanted to join them on their way to Pale. I did, and Mico Stanisic, Dragan Kijac, and chiefs of centres of public security from Sarajevo municipalities were present, as well as the representatives of the ten peripheral municipalities, commanders of police stations who were of Serb ethnicity. The meeting was brief. Mico Stanisic was introduced to us as the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska. We were told that all of us would keep their posts in Sarajevo. We were told that if a Muslim was boss he would remain to do so, but he could not issue orders to you which were contrary to the interests of the Serb people. At the time, there was no talk of any sort of classical separation of the Ministry of the Interior. Rather, since there were things happening which could not be averted, we were told that we should all keep our posts, that a minister would be appointed, that a Muslim could remain to be our superior, but that he could not ask of us to do anything that would be contrary to the interests the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talked about -- you talked about this meeting in Pale during your interview in -- in June, after you had been shown a document of a February 11th, 1992 meeting in Banja Luka. Do you remember being shown that document by the investigator? I can show it to you, if you need.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the document. I -- it was shown to me in Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we know you did not attend that meeting. And I think, in June, when you were shown the document, you said that was the first time you had seen that document about that February 11th, 1992 meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that interview, when you were asked about the date of the meeting in Pale, you said -- well, it was after -- it had to be after the February meeting. And you thought it was probably sometime in March. Today you said now late March or early April. I want to ask you, do you recollect, for example, when -- when the Serbian -- what later became the Serbian MUP or the RS MUP when Momcilo Mandic and -- and Milenko Karisik were involved in taking over the school at Vraca. Do you remember when that event occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I would like to answer the first question, and this is something that I with prove because I remembered this later on. I was issuing a denial of the lie that was published, and I provided some press clippings. I didn't go to my workplace because nobody was there at the time. I went to my flat. This was at the time when it was bombed. So that's why I think it happened in April, in early April. So, in other words, late March and -- or early April, because in the month of April, there was no one to be found there anymore. I gave you that photocopy of press clipping from Vecernje Novosti on the 7th and my denial of the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. But let me ask you a couple of questions about the meeting in Pale. Where in Pale did the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis, but I believe the witness said on the 7th and my denial of the 9th of April, 1992 and I believe -- because it appears to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know it was April 1992 that he said in his interview and I will agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my question is, the meeting in Pale that you talked about, where in Pale was the meeting held, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It was held at Kalovita Brda, formally known as the Scout's Hall. The meeting was brief. We were given the information and parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who led or chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I think it was Dragan Kijac who chaired the meeting, and I believe Mico Stanisic was present as well. Of course, this was 18 years ago, and I may be mistaken, but I would really like to give a fair statement true to what I experienced and what I remember, but I believe this was the case that Dragan Kijec chaired the meeting and that Mico Stanisic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was Mico Stanisic referred to at that meeting? Wait, don't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 33, 1, the witness say, I believe Dragan Kijac chaired that meeting and Mico Stanisic was present. I believe that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I heard too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, witness?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you said Mr. Stanisic was referred to by some position. How was he referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. I don't think that Mico Stanisic addressed the meeting. It was only Dragan Kijac who spoke. He said that a new Ministry of the Interior would be set up and that the future minister would be Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So whatever date this meeting occurred, it was before the new separate Serbian MUP had been set up and before Mico Stanisic had been made the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It is possible that this is the case, based on the conclusions from Banja Luka. But to tell you the truth, I don't know. Because minutes were compiled in Banja Luka and you gave them to me to read them, because a decision had been taken in Banja Luka that MUP of Republika Srpska would be set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your answer, it sounds like you were told at this meeting this was something that was going to happen in the future. The ministry was going to be established and Mico Stanisic was going to be made the minister at some point in the future, after the meeting. That's the way I read your answer in English. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When -- when the fighting broke out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you're going on to something new --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- this may be a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, regarding the meeting in Pale we were talking about before the break, you mentioned Mr. Kijac and Mr. Stanisic at the time meeting. Do you recall any other persons by name and position who attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I think Todor Cicovic was there an operative man, a chief of a detachment in Sokolac, which covered municipality Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Olovo, and Rogatica. Dragan Devedlaka may have been there. Goran Radovic was there, chief of the public security station from Trnovo. There were probably more people there, but it's been 18 years. It's difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the June interview, at page 20 of the transcript T001-1941 you mentioned Mr. Vlaski as well. Do you recall now if he was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was present, but I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take part at any time in writing new rules or regulations related to the -- the working of the State Security Service or I guess, in the RS MUP, it came to be called the National Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone ever ask you to take part in doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No one asked me to get involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why the name was changed from -- from state security to national security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know why the name was changed. National seems to be the same as state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were the lines of work the same in the RS MUP state security or National Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It was the same line of work, but the overall situation was changed. I don't know if we had enough capacity in terms of personnel and other resources, but mainly the lines of work were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: There was no hostile immigration, but other lines of work were the same. And there was no preparation for Defence anymore because the war had already started, and then there were no auxiliary services. Mainly we dealt with foreign intelligence services that covered various international humanitarian organisations, journalists, reporters, and there was the line of work of security for persons and facilities and some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, backtrack just for a moment. One last thing regarding the meeting in Pale. In travelling to and from Pale from Sarajevo to Pale and back, did you have any trouble getting through? Were there any roadblocks, was anybody shooting at you? Any of that going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, no. We could travel safely both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the war did break out, after Vraca was taken over around the 5th of April and shooting started seriously in Sarajevo, where were you and what did you do the rest of the month of April and up to mid-May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo. At that time, I had a bit of trouble with some lies that appeared in the newspapers. The Sarajevo -- one of the Sarajevo newspapers published a newspaper -- published an article headed: Death From the Roofs, mentioning villains, including some of my colleagues, insinuating that we were killing people around Sarajevo by sniping. And as soon as I read the article, I called the editor of that newspaper, whom I knew. I asked him where he got that information. He said he was surprised himself, but he said, I received the report and had to publish it. And then I said, Well, I insist that you publish my denial in the very next issue, tomorrow morning. And he say, Okay. If the newspaper appears at all. And I said, Why wouldn't you? And he said, Well, even if we manage to print it, you see, there's shooting in Sarajevo, we don't know if we'd be able to distribute it. But my denial appeared on the 9th of April, 1992, and Mr. Kusovac and other state security employee and the town secretary for internal affairs also published a denial. Later he moved to public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In light of what was happening at Sarajevo at the time and a newspaper article like that, did there come a time where you left your home?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I went to Grbavica to see my parents. That very day, the 7th, when I offered my denial, another lie was broadcast, this time on Yutel television and Yutel could be seen all over Yugoslavia. And I wanted to refute that one as well. And on the 9th of April, I took a team of TV reporters in to give my denial. And then came a van full of Green Berets armed with heckler guns. They arrested me and took me to a cafe not far from Bistrik and from there to the police station of Stari Grad. I was lucky inasmuch as some assistant was there named Sabovic who recognised me, and thanks to him, they let me go. I went to my home in Bistrik where I was living at the time. I spent the night there. The next day I went to attend the funeral of a neighbour of mine who had been killed. And at the funeral, I was approached by a colleague of mine who worked in the town SUP and he asked me to get out of there because these people were mainly Muslim and they had no trust in me, and I said, Where's the problem? Those were lies that were published in the newspapers and on TV and I denied that. I don't know what else I'm supposed to do. But the man kept insisting and he said, Please get away from here, go to Grbavica - that's where my parent lived - if anything, I'll call you. His name was Menso Mirojevic. He was an employee of the town SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Did you go to Grbavica? And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I spent perhaps ten days at Grbavica. I had some stomach trouble, but I managed to get my doctor on the phone. He worked in the polyclinic of the Ministry of the Interior, and I asked him to give me sick-leave to attend to my ulcer. I was there alone because I had taken my wife and children to a safe place in Hadzici, so I wanted to rejoin them, and I managed to go to Hadzici and stayed there until the 15th of May, when shells began falling, and Hadzici was held by the Serb side. The repair work-shop in Hadzici organised transport for people from Hadzici to Lukavica, which was not being shelled, but I was not allowed onto the bus because by decision of the municipality of -- or the Crisis Staff or the Presidency or whatever, no men were allowed to leave Hadzici. I tried to explain that I was not a resident of Hadzici, that I worked for the State Security Service, but the man in charge did not accept my explanations and did not let me board the bus. In the meantime, I found out that an organised group was being evacuated from Blazuj. I managed to hitch-hike my way there, and we boarded a public bus going to Pale. That was about 40 kilometres distance, but we took eight hours to get there, from 3.00 p.m. to late at night. The road across the air field was like something from an action movie. Everyone was lying down on the bus because the Muslim side kept shooting at those buses, and for the sake of their own safety all the passengers had to lie down on the floor of the bus while the bus driver zigzagged, trying to avoid bullets. I got to Pale around 1.00 a.m., and there was Slobo Skipina, Mico Stanisic, Vlasto Kusmuk, and perhaps five or six more of my colleagues. I wasn't really welcome at Pale, I have to say. Mico Stanisic told me that I have to write a statement as to where I had been until then. I said that I had not managed to drive my children to Serbia like many other people had, and my children were not safe, and I -- until I got them to a safe place -- until I got them to a safe place, I could not get to Pale. I also said that I was not born into the Ministry of the Interior and I did not have to work there, and my children mattered more to me than anything. And I thought if you -- I told them, If you need me, you know where to find me. After a couple of days, they did come for me, and that took me to Pale, that was the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where in Pale did you meet with Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Skipina, Mr. Kusmuk, and those others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: We met up at Kalovita Brda, the Kalovita hills in the scout's lodge. It was a building that was later used by the MUP because we did not have many available premises. That's where they met by day. And everyone spent the night where they could. Some people in -- took turns sleeping in some rooms that were available. Other people knew someone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the time were there any communications facilities or equipment in that building, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, there was nothing there. In that statement that I gave during proofing, I already said that we had set off from a clearing. We had only one telephone, and I also said, by way of illustration, that President Karadzic was using a car that couldn't be locked, and when he wanted to go and make a phone call, he to go to the military post office at Korana. We did not have radio stations, we did not have uniforms, or cars, or accommodation, or anything else. We did not have the basic amenities we needed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say that, are you referring to the State Security Service or the entire MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I always talk about the State Security Service, but I don't believe it was any better at the Ministry of the Interior. Meaning the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show a document. We'll put this up on the computer screen for you. It is 65 ter 2396.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if it is possible, can we have the B/C/S and the English side by side?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see that, sir? If we have the first ten name, we'll be fine.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't be possible to make it larger, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy that maybe the usher can hand you, if that's easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is entitled: Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Interior, Sarajevo National Security Service, list of employees working who were paid an advance under salaries for the month of May. And my English translation indicates number 7 is your name. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I see in the second column where there appears to be a salary figure, 65.000, yours is scratched out. Did you not get paid anything in May? Or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't remember. And even if I had received it, it was a very small amount. I don't know anymore how much it was worth, actually. As chief of the administration for the security of persons and facilities, I started working on the 1st of May, 1992. That's when the letters of appointment were written or perhaps even earlier. But, to be frank, I don't remember. I see the name of Goran Krunic is also stricken but he was there. I don't know why his name is crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say that you began working as chief of the administration for security of persons and facilities on the 1st of May. That was the date of your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I received a letter of appointment dated the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were still in Hadzici, though, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I left Hadzici on the 15th of May. But my letter of appointment is as of the 1st of May. I gave you that letter of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You gave it to me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't have it with me, but I did give it to the investigator, Mr. Paul O'Grady.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I gave him the letter of appointment for the chief and Deputy Chief of the 5th Administration, and I gave him also the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: -- certifying the termination of my employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: And the new rules on the staffing, that was the document under which I was appointed as of the 1st of May to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While you were in Hadzici before you went to Pale, had you been in any communication with anybody in -- in the Serbian MUP by telephone or some other means? I mean, how did they know where you were and what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't know where I was. Only Dragan Kijac called me up once and said, Stjeko [phoen], watch out for your own life. That's all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's while you were in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, either while I was in Grbavica or in Hadzici, but he was the only one who called me. He said, Save your skin, and watch out, and whenever you can get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise the other names on this list as people who were employed by the National Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Skipina was under-secretary for this National Security Service. But he wasn't there long. Dragan Kijac replaced him soon afterwards. Goran Radovic was there before the war. Novak Blagojevic was an inspector in the Ministry of the Interior at the administration. Todor Cicovic worked there before the war. He was chief of that detachment, I said. Number 7 is me. Dragan Kijac was there from before the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Is there any significance to the order in which these names are listed? I see number one is Mr. Skipina, and it appears that he got the biggest salary, if 75.000 is his salary. Can you detect any pattern from how the names are listed? Doesn't appear to be in alphabetical order. If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume that their order must have been that of the roles they played. Skipina was chief, Radovic and Vlaski were assistants, but I don't know who Novak Blagojevic was, under 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about Kijac? At the time, what was his job? He is number 8, right after you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Dragan Kijac was a prominent operative of the state security centre in Sarajevo. As the SDA came at the head of the MUP, Dragan Kijac was transferred to the post of an officer in charge of foreigners at the Banja Luka centre. After roughly a year there, he came back and became the secretary of the city of Sarajevo MUP. However, the post of the secretary of the town SUP was nothing really. It only had under it the traffic department, passports, duty service, and little else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could see the last page on the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could look at the back of the hard copy, witness. There's a signature on -- on the last page. The back side, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The signature is that of Slobodan Skipina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 2396.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How is this relevant, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it identifies participants and gives us some indication of the positions they held in May 1992. It will link up with other evidence in this case. We think it is important to establish who the managers are within the MUP at the time that these crimes are committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P983. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you had gone to Pale in mid-May and you are in the position of -- I guess, what's the correct title? Are you head of the 5th Administration? What was your title?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Head or chief of the administration for the security of certain individuals and facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And your duties were what? To provide protection for high-ranking individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The administration for the security of persons and facilities had to deal with the provision of security for certain office holders in the state and facilities that were important for Defence purposes. Here I'm primarily referring to the Speaker of the parliament, prime minister, and minister of the interior, and as for facilities they included Assembly or parliament facilities, Presidency facilities and government facilities as well as other facilities of importance for the defence of the country. When I assumed the position, I was governed by the prewar instructions or, rather, I tried to update the prewar instructions to the conditions under which we were working at the time. Therefore, I produced a new set of instructions on the scope of security provided to individuals and facilities, and the instructions were signed by the then minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. The instructions dealt with in detail with operative measures, technical, sanitary, and hygienic measures, as well as other forms of security to be provided. These measures were applied in such a manner as to provide full security for individuals and facilities. The designated individuals were protected by officers. There were also members of public security who mostly dealt with the physical securing of facilities and residences of the individuals who were protected. We also had scenarios for the protection of more important meetings like sessions of the parliament and government. Security escorts for travels of individuals, the security of workplaces, residences, and other premises used by the individuals who were under protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have next a question I want to ask you based on something in Exhibit P625. This is not a document you have seen before, I believe. It is the 1992 MUP draft report on the work in the period of April to December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need page 11 of the English and page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is a part of the annual report, the draft annual report that is talking about the SNB, the National Security Service. And I just want to read you a sentence and ask you a question about it. I think it's the third paragraph on your B/C/S page. And my English translation reads: "In accordance with its obligations the SNB has organised and taken measures to protect individuals, assigned protection by the relevant decisions and the facilities they use." Where it talks about "relevant decisions concerning protection of individuals," what were those, who made those decisions about who got protection, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It was always the Council for the Constitutional -- Protection of the Constitutional Order or in this case it was the Council for National Security within the parliament which took these decisions. The point is not whether Mr. So-and-so would be protected. Rather, it is the function that the person performed that was being protected. The Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order would take a decision that the role of the president, of the Presidency, or the speaker of the parliament, the prime minister, minister of the interior would be protected as well as that of other incumbents in respect of whom an assessment was made that they would come under certain -- that would be at risk in a certain situation. In addition to the facilities mentioned here, there were other facilities important for the defence of the country. For instance, the power supply facilities, power supply company facilities, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interject now. I just want to focus on individual persons. You said a decision came from the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Was that a body in the -- in the new Serbian Republic of Bosnia, what later became the Republika Srpska, or are you talking about pre-war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It existed before the war too. Presumably, the entire system of security of individuals and facilities was in place before I came to Pale. So I know that -- this was the case before the war, and I suppose it was the case when I came to Pale. Now, whether there was anything in writing from the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, I don't know about that. But I know that the Ministry of the Interior took such decisions on the basis of documents which were used before the war.
