The decision on the provision of security was something that the President of the state, the Speaker of the parliament, the prime minister would be informed of, in addition to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in the new -- in the new RS or Republika Srpska, who took the decision that the Presidency members, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, the Speaker of the Assembly Mr. Krajisnik, and the prime minister who for a while was Mr. Djeric [phoen], who took that decision, what person took that decision in the RS, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know who took this decision. I repeat: Before the war, all the functions that were mentioned here --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And your -- your unit, you and your men, at this time did you wear civilian clothes or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the witness was cut halfway through or actually he gave the answer but it was not -- it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see recorded, I don't know who took this decision. That's the answer, and he says, I repeat. He doesn't need to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, before the war all the functions that were mentioned here were protected. That's what he said -- I was trying to be helpful to you. I don't really ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who all did you in your unit protect in terms of -- if you can name the persons for me, all of the positions: The Presidency, the president of the National Assembly, and the prime minister? Anybody else? Minister of defence, minister of the justice, minister of interior, any of these lower-level cabinet --

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Neither the minister of the justice nor the minister of defence. They were not among the protected individuals. The individuals who were protected were the President of the state, Speaker of the Assembly, vice-presidents, prime minister, and minister of the interior. And, where necessary, the minister of defence was also provided security but he normally received it from his own members. The minister of the interior never provided security for the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally or anybody in your 5th Administration provide protection to Minister Stanisic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The administration for security of individuals and facilities did not provide security for the minister of the interior. Why? Well, because he was always on the payroll of the security service. I don't know how to explain -- always on the payroll of public security, so he always received his salary from the Public Security Service, and it was always the public security employees who provided security for the minister of the interior. Just as was the case before the war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat slowly what he just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters ask if you could repeat slowly what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Even before the war, the minister of the interior, including the minister of the interior during the war was on the payroll of the Public Security Service. So, I said, that by way of an example before the war, the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina received his salary from the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the under-secretary for state security received his salary from the Government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1992, did Mico Stanisic have any personal security, either an individual or a detail, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: As of the 15th of May when I came to Pale, Mico Stanisic had his personal security provided by individuals who were members of the Public Security Service. In other words, the members of my administration did not provide security to Mico Stanisic. He was provided that service by members of the Public Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what specific unit or individuals provided that service? Were they from a particular administration or particular group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: They were members of the Public Security Service. The only thing I know is that Zoran Jasarevic was Mico Stanisic's driver. He lived at Pale. There were other members of the Public Security Service who were his escort, but I don't know his name. I noticed among the security detail for Mico Stanisic a fellow who was rather imposing in his figure. I knew his father. What was his family name? I knew that soon thereafter he was killed, but I don't know which year that was. I think his last name was Malovic. And I believe that those who knew Minister better than I did, said that he used to be a member of the Yugoslav Army but that he had left the army. I don't know where he served. Perhaps in Croatia or Slovenia. And that he was later transferred to the security detail for Minister Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 65 ter 2686 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would kindly ask Mr. Hannis to make pauses between question and response by the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you see this document which purports to be a salary list for the Special Platoon Sokolac in October 1992. The first name is Dusko Malovic. Is that the person you were telling us about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I presume so. But under 26, you have another Malovic. Though it must be the one under number 1, Dusko Malovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you come to know who Dusko Malovic was in -- in 1992? Can you tell us when and where you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I think that I saw him first outside the Assembly or the Presidency, because he was quite a striking figure. He was of -- well-built physique, and I asked around about that fellow who was accompanying minister and they told me that it was Malovic from Sokolac who used to be a member of the army. I don't know if he was in Croatia and then left the army at which point he joined the security detail for Mr. Stanisic. Perhaps they knew each other from before the war. Perhaps they were good mates, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this first time you saw him outside the Presidency or the Assembly, was that in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was at Pale in the building at Kalovita hills. I saw him two, three, or four times, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And all of those times were in Pale, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Pale. He probably accompanied the minister across Republika Srpska. I only had occasion to see him at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in Pale, did you see him with the minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how --

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: In other words, he would accompany the minister, and then the minister would go into to see either the Speaker of the parliament or the President or one of the ministers, and he would be -- he would always stay behind with the driver, waiting for the minister to finish his business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how was -- how was he dressed and equipped?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes he would be wearing civilian clothes, other times a camouflage uniform. It depended on where they were supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: His camouflage uniform, you notice anything particular about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I didn't observe anything particular about it. Of course, the first sets of camouflage uniforms that arrived were the ones worn by ministers and the personnel around them, and we all envied them, because we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it standard issue, or was it of higher quality than the average, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was the first time we saw camouflage uniforms to begin with. They had not previously existed and were not in use by our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to the 15th of the May? Is that what you're saying, there were no camouflage uniforms on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were no camouflage uniforms. And when I'm saying our army, I meant the Yugoslav People's Army which had the solid colour olive-grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit P29 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could I have this 2686 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit Number P984, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a -- I'm sorry. This is a copy of a news article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis, before you go on, this is being -- you asked this to be marked for identification pending ... pending what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that this witness can verify the authenticity of this document. I may need somebody from finance or somebody who signed the document. I -- if there's no objection I will tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I suppose the relevance of this is the same as your answer was to my previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in particular, I'm going to show that Dusko Malovic was employed by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, you see the photograph? Could we enlarge? And perhaps you can read the caption under the photograph for us. Can you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you read it out loud for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: "Members of the service of Serb ethnicity were invited to join the Serbian MUP as early as today. Delimustafic called on the need for unity. Those who leave will be dismissed. April Fool's reality."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The small print under the photograph, are you able to read that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: "EPA published this photograph yesterday. The advisor of the MUP of BH Mico Stanisic in the role of the minister of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BH is reviewing members of the Serbian MUP at Sokolac."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know this photograph is not the best quality. Can you tell if those men are wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I suppose they are wearing them, although you can't really tell from the photograph. Can I add something? The April Fool's reality, do you think anybody was really worried by what Delimustafic stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm just asking about the photograph for now. Maybe Defence counsel will have a question about that. Do you see anybody else that you recognise in the photograph, other than Mico Stanisic, whom I think we can all recognise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I know very well Mico Stanisic. And the fellow that Mico Stanisic is shaking hands with and might be Dusko Malovic, because, as I can see in the photograph, it is a rather imposing figure. I'm not sure, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I want to ask you now about 1992. You told us, I think, when you first started out in -- in Pale that Mr. Skipina was your boss in the SNB?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Skipina was the person with the most extensive experience compared to the others on the list that you gave me. He was the chief of national security, later on, to become the chief of public security, and was retired before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at Exhibit P823, if we may. And your next boss after Skipina in 1992 was who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: After Skipina, Dragan Kijac became the head of the administration for national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I know the B/C/S copy is maybe hard to read on screen. Are you able to read it? I know have you looked at it before. I can give you a hard copy, if that might be easier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: A hard copy might be better. I received a copy of this at Herceg-Novi when I was giving my statement in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see in my English translation that it is dated the 13th of August and it appears to be from Dragan Kijac with a signature and a stamp informing that on the 6th of August, Dragan Kijac was appointed SNB under-secretary thereby replacing former SNB under-secretary Slobodan Skipina. Have I two questions for you: Is it unusual for the person who is being appointed to send out the notification that he is being appointed and replacing someone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I said that back in Herceg-Novi. There's something illogical about this. Wouldn't it have been more logical for the minister of the interior to have written an order or a dispatch informing all security services centres both public and state security, that this is an appointment of Dragan Kijac for the chief of the CSB. This way it looks like Dragan Kijac informs himself that from this day on, he is the secretary -- the under-secretary for state security. And he signs it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. I have a question about the second paragraph which says: "In accordance with the conclusions of the SNB specialist staff no appointments to the Service" --

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: "Of the professional collegium."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "No appointments to the Service shall be possible in future without their approval." Do you know who the members of that specialist collegium in the SNB were, either by name or by position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Members of the professional collegium are, as a rule the under- secretary for state security, his deputies, assistants, and chiefs of administration. That's the narrow composition, and the broader includes the under-secretary for state security, his deputy and assistant. In fact, the collegium of the State Security Service consists of all chiefs of sectors of state security and all centres in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does the minister of the interior, Mr. Stanisic, have the power to override or veto decisions of the specialist collegium concerning appointments, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I suppose that for every important post in the Ministry of the Interior, the minister must be informed. Or at least must be consulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't think the minister would have the final word? Do you think the specialist board could appoint somebody that the minister did not approve of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, the minister always has the last word. But it make a big difference who the minister is. If the minister is someone who has -- who is not a career minister -- a career professional, it's quite different. I had quite embarrassing experiences with ministers who occupy the position without knowing anything about professional matters. I'm consulting him about a professional matter and he is talking on the phone about some logs that need to be transported from one end of the country to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had understood you to say in an earlier interview that you believe the minister would be the one with the final word about any appointments; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the minister always has the final word. The under-secretary for state security is duty-bound to inform the minister about any steps and measures he plans to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you Exhibit 65 ter 3367. Witness, this is a document that you were shown during your interview in June 2009. It's a very lengthy document. I don't propose to show you the whole thing. Just from that cover page do you remember this document that Investigator Grady showed you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know, I remember the document. This was the duty service log-book in the Kikinda building I recognise the signature of Cicovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's fair to say there appears to be handwriting of several different persons in this log-book, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are several different persons depending on who was on duty at the time or who took the call and took down the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But based on content and the writing of Mr. Cicovac that you recognised, you -- you came to opine that this was a duty log for the Kikinda building in 1992 and 1992? Or part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was housed in Kikinda in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, Dr. Karadzic was accommodated in Kikinda, the President of the Assembly, and some of the ministers. After the building at Kalovita Brda was renovated, Dr. Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik, as Speaker of the Assembly, moved there, and perhaps a year later, the office of the President of the republic was housed in the Famos building in Koran. That's perhaps a kilometre away from the centre of Pale. The special purpose industry was located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately when Karadzic moved out of Kikinda?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I think it was towards the end of 1992 or perhaps the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't think we made it clear. Kikinda was a hotel in Pale before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, Kikinda, was a prefab building of -- of a construction company from Serbia, the town of Kikinda, and that's why we named it Kikinda, after that enterprise. It was a building -- in fact, a recreational facility for the personnel of this Serbian company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple of other buildings in Pale I want to ask you about. Hotel, well, Panorama?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Panorama was, indeed, a hotel. I mean, what do you call a hotel? It was a very poor category of a hotel, but ... the last category.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who stayed in the Panorama Hotel between May and December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The Speaker of the Assembly was accommodated there. Some employees of a number of ministries. I think some of the ministers even for a while. But for a very short while, because, in 1992, the government was moved to the Bistrica Hotel at Pale. I know that by the time winter set on, they were in Bistrica Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Kosuta hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Kosuta was a hotel owned by a very large conglomerate called Energoinvest based in Sarajevo, and I think they built the hotel. Or maybe not. Because next to that hotel were apartments, suites for employees of Energoinvest. The whole complex was built for the Winter Olympic games in Sarajevo in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what persons or organisations were housed in that hotel in May to December of 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear? You mean Kosuta hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I think the special detachment of the police of the MUP was based there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with your work as chief of security for persons and facilities, did you co-ordinate with anyone on the public security side regarding security of buildings; and, if so, who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to co-operate on a daily basis. I already told you that this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter is asking for you to repeat. So I wanted to stop you before you got too far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had to co-operate with the public security sector on a daily basis, both with the police stations which covered the territory where the buildings were, in this case, the police station in Pale and the company for OBL which was in charge of physical security of buildings and apartments of VIPs. The police station was in charge of patrolling routes, and OBL was in charge of traditional physical security of buildings and apartments housing VIPs, buildings that were venues of important events such as sessions of the Assembly, the government, the Presidency, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning security of the buildings, for example, in Hotel Bistrica where the government was for a period in 1992, was there any rule or prohibition against carrying weapons into the Hotel Bistrica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning there was no such ban, but, later, when we acquired some equipment such as metal-detecting doors and some anti-sabotage equipment for the post office, everyone had to deposit their weapons in specially designated lockers or other places. Nobody could go in and attend the sessions armed, apart from one or two guards who were inside the hall. Everyone was accredited and went offering their letters of accreditation. They would have to deposit their weapons until they left the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you said that changed later on, can you tell us approximately what month did it change that weapons could no longer be brought in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: As soon as we acquired these metal-detector doors, after the first two or three months, that was for the building of the Presidency first, and then, also, for the office of Radovan Karadzic, in that Famos building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talking about in Bistrica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: In Bistrica, you could go in with a weapon. The government was housed there, as well as some of the ministers, including the prime minister. Some ministers were not housed in Bistrica but in some other locations, but in Bistrica, yes, you could walk -- walk in armed because there was no one but members of the government there, just the ministers and the personnel who serviced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The last thing, Your Honours, I would like to tender 65 ter 3367. That was the log-book -- well, I don't want to tender it at this point. I guess I need to mark it MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That was a lengthy document [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a lengthy document. The witness indicated it appeared to be the duty-log book at Kikinda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You propose to tender that as an exhibit at some future point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, pending connecting it up with certain persons and showing some relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for the witness at this time. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit Number P985. Thank you. Marked for identification, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is coincidently the time that we would take the break, so we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, it would be convenient to -- to give this oral ruling on this other question. And that is on -- it goes as follows: On the 29th of January, the Trial Chamber granted the addition of ST-216 to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber also ordered the Prosecution to make submissions regarding whether it would seek to call the witness viva voce or pursuant to Rule 92 ter and on the time it would need for each mode of testimony. On the 3rd of February, the Prosecution filed further submissions. The Prosecution states that it will call ST-216 viva voce and request the Chamber to allow three hours for the examination-in-chief, thus extending by three hours the time allotted for the presentation of the Prosecution's evidence in-chief. The Trial Chamber grants the request to call the witness viva voce. However, it notes that the Prosecution has not identified in its further submissions any new matters on which the witness would testify which would justify the three hours requested. The Chamber, therefore, grants the Prosecution two hours for the examination-in-chief of ST-216. The time allotted to the Prosecution's evidence in-chief is, therefore, extended to 216 hours. Any further time that the Prosecution wishes to use in presenting the evidence of ST-216 is to be found within the 216 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Scekic. If I understood correctly, I think you were employed in the State Security Service from 1979, the State Security Service of the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After these multi-party elections in 1991 and the personnel changes that happened in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 and beginning 1992, there occurred an extreme marginalisation of Serb staff in the MUP in general, but especially in the State Security Service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. A certain Hilmo Selimovic became chief of personnel and he came from the brewery, the beer factory, and he served about 300 new letters of appointment, and he changed the secretary for state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We really have to make pauses between question and answer to enable interpretation. When you say Hilmo Selimovic came -- became chief of personnel in the MUP, in the State Security Service, and he handed out three new -- 300 new letters of appointment in one day, you mean decisions on employment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, on employment, new employment, and also replacements, demotions. He demoted mainly Serb staff, and perhaps a few of his fellow Muslims, but mainly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Similarly, all these new decisions on new hiring were in favour of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. A great number of people whom we had never laid eyes on before came to work with us. I'm only talking about the place where I worked, but I believe in other sectors it was not much different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Novic, whom you mentioned a moment ago, who by decision of this same Selimovic was demoted to one of the lowest positions, had been under-secretary for state security of Bosnia-Herzegovina until then, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So from the highest ladder in the hierarchy he was demoted to the lowest one, although, at that moment, he already had in his hands a letter of appointment transferring him to the federal SUP in Belgrade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. He was to become federal under-secretary for state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sredoje Novic was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sredoje Novic is currently minister in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, for civil affairs in the ministerial council of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before that he was minister of the interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said, "Federation," it must have been a slip. You meant the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One of the key positions in the State Security Service was then occupied by Munir Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He became chief of sector of the state security. It was the highest-ranking sector in the Republic, and everything was charted from that base, from the base in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "charted," you mean various operations of the State Security Service. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I meant that, and I meant also the media harangue against us, who were not part of his ethnic community. Munir Alibabic was a great professional, very good in his trade, and if I have time, I will also say something about the then-president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic that concerns Munir Alibabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We've already heard here, but we could repeat it. You are probably mean the fact that Munir Alibabic, in his time, led the operation to arrest Alija Izetbegovic. Is that what you mean, in the 1970s?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the main person responsible in the service for that operation. Alija Izetbegovic was put on trial in 1983, and he was sentenced to 13 or 16 years in prison because of his Islamic declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when Munir Alibabic was made chief it was a great surprise to all of you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It certainly was. Because while Alija Izetbegovic was in prison, Munir Alibabic became his close collaborator, and I believe those ties were formed then and that's why he made him chief of -- of state security but at the same time, we couldn't understand what was going on like we didn't understand many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned the media harangue. It is your opinion that Munir Alibabic was behind the media harangue, as you put it, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where he demonised or placed false -- planted false information in relation to the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I experienced it first-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the media," I suppose you mean that Munir Alibabic, from the post that he held of the chief of state security, he wielded great influence over the media, such as Slobodna Bosna or Oslobodjenje and television?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Munir Alibabic had worked for a while for radio and television as an operative. In line 03 he had connections in the mass media. You mentioned Slobodna Bosna, and it is quite possible that he had close ties with journalists from Slobodna Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you experienced this first-hand, I think that it was in early April, around the 7th of April, if I'm not mistaken, that in some of the daily newspapers, an untrue story was published which ostracised you personally. Several days later, another untrue story was broadcast on TV and again it had to do with you, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this article which was published in Sarajevo Vecernje entitled: Death From Roof-tops, and the information broadcast in the Utro [as interpreted] show both conveyed accounts that you were untrue. I issued denials on both occasions. Nevertheless, I was arrested by the Green Berets, the Muslim paramilitary organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The truth of the matter is that the information that was planted about you was untrue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All of it was a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I recollect correctly your statement for the Prosecution, your own brother is married to a Muslim and has lived all of his life in Sarajevo and has spent the war in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the reserve force of the police in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, statements to the effect that you were a Serb or a Montenegrin nationalist were completely baseless; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. In the building where my parents live, they had a neighbour who lived upstairs from them, and although she had children at Miljacka she did not want to leave because she wanted to stay close to my parents. My wife was a physician, an anaesthesiologist, she worked for a hospital, and I've brought this letter along for the sake of the Prosecution. This letter was written by him as a thank-you note because he wanted to indicate how a Serb treated people of other ethnicities. I don't know if you're interested, but it would be a good thing to read the letter aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, let me cut this short. We don't want to complicate matters further. You see, we have a procedure in place for such documents. If I understand you correctly, the letter was sent by a Muslim who was hospitalised on the ward where your wife worked, and this was his way of saying thank you for the humane and fair treatment that he received from your wife.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please read slowly and start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read out his name only. We don't need the address. But, please, do it slowly for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: The letter was written by Asim Ajanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Back in 1979 when you started working, you worked for the sector for defence preparations in the State Security Service in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under defence preparations, what is meant are plans drawn up for -- for a state of war or of an immediate threat of war in accordance with the then-Laws on All People's Defence and civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Such plans were drafted by and involved at least 2 million people in the former state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "2 million people," you're actually referring to the fact that every institution and every socio-political community from the lowest to the highest level had to have such plans in accordance with the principles of All People's Defence and social protection. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, every socio-political organisation and community had to produce such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, such plans were also made by the army and the police. Plans for emergency situations were drafted by the army and police alike. Every school had to have one such plan. There wasn't a single public institution that didn't have a plan of the sort. The concept of All People's Defence was to defend one's self from an external aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to April 1992. It is a fact, is it not, that you went to work and continued going to work at the time when untrue information was published about you on TV and in the press.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: At the time I no longer went to work. Following the meeting at Pale when we were told that we should resume our posts, I intended to do precisely that. However, around the MUP building, I saw individuals who were people with secondary school, who were armed, and they circled around the building, and when I saw them, I didn't want to proceed going to the office. So I went back home and then what happened next was that there was a gun-shot that went right through my window and then everything else happened that I already recounted to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, based on what you heard at the meeting, you proceeded to go to your office and work for the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, the first time you tried to enter the building, you encounter in front of it, some of your colleagues, technicians, et cetera, carrying long-barrelled weapons and performing some sort of a security detail outside of the building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it occurs to us that the issue that would have arisen because of the Prosecution's application, that inasmuch as we assume, that in order to deal with this, you would need time to consult with your client, whether it is something that you propose to do in the course of today, which, having regard to the fact that we are in an evening sitting would mean that would you have to do it before the ordinary time that we adjourn at 7.00, or is it something that you propose to do in the morning, in which case we might consider, on your application, a later than usual start, or is it something which, on reflection, no longer causes you a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm grateful to Your Honours for -- for this. I have -- I have consulted with my client during the breaks to a certain extent. I would definitely appreciate if -- if I could have an additional half an hour to one hour in the morning, so we can start at 10.00. That would be really very good -- very good time for me to be able to consult properly with the client, with all the documents which I intend to show and all that. So if it pleases the Court, then the 10.00 in the morning would go be perfect more me, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And still finish with this witness by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, by all mean, Your Honours. I will -- I will finish with the witness within first hour -- I will leave only probably this issue for tomorrow so ... So I might need half an hour, I guess, or 45 minute, maximum. Maybe even much lesser than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, arrangements would be made for your client to be brought in, the usual time, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you mentioned these colleagues of yours who were standing outside the building of the State Security Service where you were working at the time, these colleagues were all Muslims or Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after finding yourself unable to go inside to your office, you went back home and found out that your apartment had been shot at.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that's one of the first bullets fired at a residential building. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the first bullet fired at an apartment. I went in, immediately the telephone rang, foul language used, We will buy a ticket, send you to Montenegro. The person hung up. I tried to plaster this whole shot, went downstairs, found some Muslim neighbours standing there, asked them what was going on, and they were saying, The Chetniks are shooting. And I said, Why would the Chetniks be shooting at a Serb apartment? But they insisted, Yes, they are Chetniks and Chetniks. I took the bullet out of my pocket and said, Look, neighbours and friends, bullets don't choose. This was fired at my apartment. And then I took my leave and no longer went back to my apartment until I had that encounter with the TV crew from Yutel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this return to your apartment with the TV crew, after the TV crew left, you were arrested by the Green Berets, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We just discussed this meeting at Pale, and you said that in keeping with what you'd heard at that meeting, you went to work. Obviously that meeting took place just before the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with any certainty. I believe it was in the end of March, early April. More probably in early April, because of these things that happened to me with the newspaper articles and the TV programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence in-chief, my colleague asked you and correlated you with that meeting referring to the minutes of the meeting in Banja Luka, they showed you that in July when they interviewed you at your residence. You never attended that meeting in Banja Luka, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't even know that it was held.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And never before the Prosecution showed you the minutes did you know that there were minutes, let alone seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what's written in the minutes of that meeting from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I saw the minutes for the first time in June, when it was showed to me by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal in Herceg-Novi, when I was giving my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when they showed you that document, I suppose you told them you had never seen it before. I suppose the only -- they only asked you to identify some of the persons who attended that meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I knew most of them, because they were my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know any more about it. You don't know what the conclusions of that meeting were and what was decided?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: No, I was just shown a list of people who attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you are unable to correlate the meeting in Banja Luka and the meeting that you attended in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: I can only guess. The first time they called me, I went to Pale. That meeting was short. It was said that the minister of the interior would be Mico Stanisic, that we should all resume our work, that assignments that run counter to the interests of Serbian people cannot be issued by the chief, et cetera. That was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once, when you were talking about this, you said that Dragan Kijac, your colleague from the State Security Service, chaired that meeting, that the meeting related to the area of the CSB Sarajevo. That is to say, all the 20 municipalities, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, at that meeting - and this is on page 30, lines 19 and 20 - Dragan Kijac introduced Mico Stanisic as the new minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Observation, that misstates his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry, I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, his evidence was he going to be the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I have a citation of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can I hear the objection, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My objection is that misstates the evidence. I need to make a page reference to the prior transcript what he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I made the page reference. It's page 30, lines 19 and 20 of today's transcript. 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that the only reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic was introduced to us as the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska. That is why I gave the reference and the witness confirmed. And let me please continue my cross-examination. If I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hannis is right, after that, on page 33, line 15, you stated: "The future minister." He was introduced as the future minister. So you allow the possibility that you do not remember precisely how he was introduced, whether he was the minister as of that moment, or the minister to be.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, really, it was almost 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. A moment ago, towards the end of your evidence in-chief, you talked about the introduction of these metal-detector doors in Pale at Mount Jahorina and in some buildings. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. We used those doors for buildings located there, and we also moved them as required when Assembly sessions were held elsewhere, such as in the Famos building at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, since you were in charge of security of buildings in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it true that all important buildings that you secured in Sarajevo were equipped with those metal-detecting doors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Well, state agencies had them. But, more important, business facilities did not. The Presidency had them, however, the government buildings, the Assembly, Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm being told that on page 75, line 10 and 11, the witness gave a lengthier answer than was recorded. He said it was almost 20 years ago, and he allows for both possibilities concerning whether Mr. Stanisic was introduced as the current minister or the minister to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually say that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, as you were discussing with my learned friend Mr. Hannis you said one thing that aroused my interest. You said that in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the ministers' pay was provided by the Assembly, and that of the under-secretary for state security by the government.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe the under-secretary was better paid than the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I want to ask you. In the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, former, I mean, Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia, the position of under-secretary for state security was always a bit stronger than the -- that of the secretary for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a key person. We had a very strict hierarchy. The under-secretary for state security informed the minister of the interior only selectively, only about certain things. And in sometimes before the war, he had to keep informed the President of the Central Committee, the President of the Presidency, and possibly the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that the under-secretary for internal affairs had the job primarily of informing the highest state authorities. I mean, the under-secretary for state security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was his job. But sometimes he would go through the minister. It all depended on who the minister was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes that minister was actually someone who was not from the service, who occupied a major position in -- in the economy before that. It all depended on whether he was a professional or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that care was always taken that the under-secretary for state security should always be someone from the service, a professional?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: It had to be someone from the -- the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the professional had to come from the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While the post of the minister could have been occupied by a politician who happened to assume that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dusko Gojan was a minister for many years and he started as an operative and ended up as a minister. He was replaced by a man who had previously been at the head of the pension and social security fund. He again was replaced by a policeman who used to have a large private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the head of the pension fund assumed this post, you're referring to the predecessors of Delimustafic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the last individual you mentioned, a policeman who had a large private business you're actually referring to Minister Delimustafic, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The gentleman who came from the pension fund, do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC
utterances.text: Muhamed Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed the portion of my examination that I previously planned before the scope of his testimony was expanded to include Dusko Malovic's unit. Perhaps I should stop here and resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the remaining -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We were just wondering in terms of maximizing time whether the remaining half-hour today might be utilized by counsel, Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as the matters stand now we will not have any questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to bring to your attention, Your Honours, we may need to notify victim witness to bring the witness later tomorrow if we're going to have a late start, and I don't know if there's anybody around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will take the adjournment now until 10.00 in the morning, and the Registry should make the necessary arrangements to have the accused, particularly Stanisic, here at what ordinarily would have been the commencement time tomorrow, to allow his counsel to consult with him, in order to facilitate his further cross-examination of this witness. The -- the -- and, Mr. Witness, you will forgive if I don't attempt to call you by -- by your proper name, but you are still under oath, sworn as a witness, and I am -- would remind you that the -- having been so sworn, that you cannot communicate with counsel from either side, nor in your communications with anyone outside of the court, can you discuss your testimony, the -- the testimony that you are giving. So the Court will now rise, and you are excused as a witness, but you are not released. And those responsible for your transportation will ensure that you are back before the Tribunal so that it can resume your testimony at 10.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of February, 2010, at 10.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
